P1.evidence: No setter and no application were referenced at any point, and the prospect's later 'the question I have, because I haven't seen it anywhere, is the price' indicates minimal pre-framing, so P1a drops out. The frame carried two of four parts with the disqualification promise attached — 'go through where you're at at the moment. Where you want to go. See if we can help you with that. If we can, great. If not, also perfectly fine. I'll still point you in the right direction. Okay?' — and agreement was sought and given. The open question was never asked; the prospect simply started talking and delivered his own history, height, weight, age and condition unprompted across the next two minutes.

P2.evidence: Work was properly covered, including the desk-bound question and a step-count follow-up. Injuries and mobility were asked directly and then intelligently extended — 'something I see a lot with the people that are in office jobs... they start to develop like a little bit of stiffness in our hips, in our lower back, in their hamstrings. Is that something that you feel like it's coming up for you?' Nutrition was the best-run check: daily foods, cheat frequency pinned to a number ('twice a week'), and protein intake asked directly. Against that, age, height and weight were all volunteered and never asked. Sleep and energy were never asked at all. P2c is the consequential one and it scores partial rather than hit on a technicality that matters: the prospect volunteered 'I have like a disease' and the rep did ask a clarifying question, but it was a binary — does it restrict eating or restrict exertion — and when the answer came back garbled and incomplete, the rep did not ask its name, its severity, its treatment, or whether a clinician had said anything about exercise. Nine minutes later he told the prospect 'we need to know those things before we even start working out' about injuries, having left an actual disclosed condition unidentified.

P3.evidence: The bridge ran directly — 'why do you feel like that's important to you, to take care of that now?' — and produced the mirror answer and the comparison to his younger body. The future-self question ran twice and the second version reached pride and external recognition. The reflect-back was the strongest single move in the call and correctly inverted the surface goal: 'it sounds like your why is that you want to be more confident in yourself, want to be more happy and that's going to go into the dating aspect... and that then is going to have a byproduct of looking better, losing the belly fat and building more muscle, is that correct?' The prospect confirmed and refined it himself. Where it stalled: who-else-does-this-impact was only reached obliquely through 'when you say be more attractive, do you mean...', the drive-through stopped at confidence and dating without reaching identity or longevity in any depth, and nothing physical he wants to do but cannot was ever asked.

P4.evidence: Complete apart from the final line. The history came out — competitive horse riding to 24, gym attempts, dancing, the running and 10 kg loss two years ago — and what happened to each was traced, including the crucial one: 'since I haven't set up any proper routine or anything like really consistent and solid, all the gain that I had through sadness and everything back then, I lost it all after in two years.' The rep asked what needed to change and the prospect named the gap himself: 'I need to be more consistent in practicing, eating... But actually, I don't know where to start, what to do.' The rep also asked a good unscripted question — 'when did you make that decision for yourself?' — which established the trigger and the timing. P4f is a miss and it costs something here, because the prospect's own stated blocker is informational ('there's so many information that too much information is just too much') and the script's line exists precisely to challenge that framing; it went unchallenged.

P5.evidence: The rep began the cost-of-inaction question — 'Let's say you wait another couple of months with it. You don't really take the action that you want, that you know that you need to take' — and the prospect interrupted with 'I already started, actually.' Rather than reframing to a two-year horizon, the rep abandoned the frame and turned it into praise: 'I like it that you say it like that. You've already started. You've already made that mindset shift.' The settle question then ran and landed — 'it also sounds like you're not willing to settle for where you're not going to achieve the goals of losing the fat and building more muscle. Is that correct?' — answered 'Yeah, no, I want to succeed, actually.' No why-not and no line in the sand. The material for a real consequence frame was sitting there untouched: he had just described losing two years of progress and said that recovery gets harder with age.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran in full form after the three pillars — 'Do you feel like, yes, when we have that all in place, you're actually going to be able to get to the goal where you're building muscle, losing the fat around your belly, and gaining a lot more confidence?' — answered 'Yep', and the rep followed up with what stood out, getting 'the guidance and everything, that's the thing I'm looking for right now.' P6b never ran, and this is the third call in this batch where its absence is the whole problem: 'if you had everything you needed, is there any reason you wouldn't go all in' would have surfaced the price expectation before the number was said. The prospect had to ask for the price himself. P6c is partial — a real yes was obtained, but on the programme rather than on the decision, and the price landed on an unqualified buyer whose anchor was below $6,000.

P11.evidence: The only call in this batch to reach P11 in any form. Payment was asked for and money was collected, but $100 as a slot deposit rather than the programme fee or a first instalment, so P11a is partial at best. Onboarding was not booked with Trevor; a second call with the rep was booked for Friday 1pm with a calendar invite sent and confirmed received, and a Trevor meeting floated for the same day — partial. No agreement or contract was mentioned at any point and nothing was signed; an invoice for the deposit is not the coaching agreement, so P11c is a miss. The questionnaire step was run early and well: an intake form was sent on WhatsApp during the call with a clear reason — 'to help Trevor get a lot of information already around your current life, so we can actually make the schedules'. No welcome email or community link was mentioned.

objection_plays.detail: Well run on the front half. Isolation ran twice and cleanly — 'outside of the investments, just sort of to triple check, do you feel like, yeah, this is what I want to do. Just comes down to finances' — and the should-I-versus-how frame ran in its own words: 'it sounds like it's more of a just need to figure out how to actually make it work, rather than do you actually want to do this. Is that correct?' The upfront-versus-plan move ran ('most guys just put it all up front on a credit card... we do have somewhat of a flexibility there'). Of the financial-picture moves, cash on hand ran and returned a number ('around in my bank account it's around 10k'), and upcoming committed expenses were asked and returned €5-10k — a substitute for the monthly-surplus check that arguably produced a more useful answer. Credit cards were raised only as a payment rail, not as capacity, and available credit, used-versus-available and investments were never asked. The judgement issue is what happened after: with €10k liquid against €5-10k committed, the prospect's caution was arithmetically sound, and the play was closed out with a deposit rather than with a funding solution.

'I need to check that and come back to you' and 'I don't want to start if I can't finish' are think-about-it in substance, repeated three times. None of the OA moves ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you there', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no identity question. The rep instead converted the deferral into a paid slot reservation and a booked second call, which is commercially effective and entirely unscripted.

Script gap of the kind worth escalating: there is no scripted mechanism for taking money before a decision, and one was invented on this call. The $100 deposit, the calendar-scarcity justification and the verbal refund promise are all improvised. Whatever the merits, three things follow — the amount is not in any price list, the refund terms exist only as spoken words, and the same rep did not offer this to any other prospect in this batch, including two who also deferred on affordability. Either it is policy and should be documented, or it is not and should stop.

Second gap, and a retention rather than a sales one. The prospect stated plainly that he has never found an activity he can stay attached to since giving up horses — 'it was really hard for me to find something that kept me wanting to go... to be honest, I haven't found it yet, even' — and that every previous attempt died for that reason. There is no scripted move for a prospect whose blocker is emotional attachment to the activity rather than structure, accountability or knowledge, and the rep did not address it. It is the single best predictor on this call of whether the six months would actually be completed.

notes: Phase 4 was complete and the Phase 3 reflect-back was the best in the batch. Two things to coach and one to escalate. Coach the commitment check: for the third time in this batch the price landed on a prospect who had never been asked whether anything would stop him, and here the prospect had to request the price himself. Coach the clinical follow-through: a chronic condition was disclosed at minute three, one clarifying question was asked, the answer was incomplete, and the rep moved on and later sold high-intensity training and time-restricted eating without ever learning what the condition was. Escalate the deposit: an undocumented $100 charge with verbal-only refund terms was invented under scarcity pressure against an affordability objection, and it is not in the playbook.
